title: Basic Structure Doctrine
points: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-judge bench (7:6) — Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure
Later cases: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980), S.R. Bommai (1994), I.R. Coelho (2007)
Basic features recognised include supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, federalism, secularism, free and fair elections, rule of law
explanation: Judge-made limit on Parliament's amending power under Article 368. Any constitutional amendment (and, in some cases, ordinary law) violating the basic structure can be struck down. The Constitution never defines 'basic structure' — courts identify features case by case. Exam hook: 'Which case propounded the doctrine?' → Kesavananda Bharati; 'Which amendment sought to curb judicial review and was struck down in Minerva Mills?' → 42nd Amendment (parts of Art. 368 clauses 4 & 5).

title: Article 21 — Right to Life & Personal Liberty
points: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law'
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): procedure must be fair, just and reasonable (links Arts 14, 19, 21)
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017): 9-judge bench — Right to Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21
Olga Tellis (1985): right to livelihood; Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002): free education 6–14 years
explanation: Article 21 is the most expansive fundamental right. Through judicial interpretation it now covers privacy, dignity, health, clean environment, speedy trial, free legal aid, and livelihood. It is available against the State (and can be enforced via Article 32/226 writs). It cannot be suspended even during Emergency (44th Amendment protects Arts 20 and 21 under Art. 359).

title: Article 14 — Equality before Law
points: 'Equality before law' (British concept) + 'equal protection of the laws' (American concept)
Permissible classification: intelligible differentia + rational nexus with the object
E.P. Royappa (1974) & Maneka Gandhi: arbitrariness is antithetical to equality; Shayara Bano (2017) applied 'manifest arbitrariness'
explanation: Article 14 applies to all persons (citizens and non-citizens), including legal persons. The test of 'reasonable classification' permits differential treatment where the classification is based on an intelligible differentia and has a rational relation to the object sought. The 'arbitrariness' test treats unreasonable State action as violating equality.

title: Article 32 — Constitutional Remedies
points: Dr B.R. Ambedkar: 'heart and soul of the Constitution'
Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
Supreme Court (Art. 32) — for Fundamental Rights only; High Courts (Art. 226) — for Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose'
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and part of the basic structure
explanation: Writ jurisdiction lets a person directly approach the Supreme Court if a Fundamental Right is violated. Habeas corpus = 'produce the body'; Mandamus = 'we command'; Certiorari = quash orders of lower bodies; Prohibition = stop a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction; Quo warranto = 'by what authority' a public office is held.

title: Judicial Review
points: Derived from Articles 13, 32, 131–136, 143, 226, 246 and 372
Marbury v. Madison (1803, USA) is the origin of the modern doctrine
L. Chandra Kumar (1997): judicial review is part of basic structure; Tribunals' decisions are subject to HC scrutiny
Ninth Schedule laws enacted after 24 April 1973 are open to review (I.R. Coelho, 2007)
explanation: Judicial review is the power of courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts and to declare them void if they violate the Constitution. Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void.

title: Collegium System & NJAC
points: Evolved through the Three Judges Cases: S.P. Gupta (1981), Second Judges (1993), Third Judges Reference (1998)
Collegium for SC: CJI + 4 senior-most judges; for HCs: CJI + 2 senior-most judges
99th Amendment & NJAC Act, 2014 were struck down in the Fourth Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association, 2015)
explanation: The collegium is a judge-made system of appointment and transfer of judges, not found in the Constitution (Articles 124 and 217 only say the President appoints 'after consultation'). Exam hook: NJAC would have comprised CJI, two senior SC judges, Law Minister and two eminent persons.

title: Article 370 verdict (2023)
points: In re: Article 370 of the Constitution (11 December 2023): a 5-judge Constitution Bench unanimously upheld the 2019 abrogation
Held that Article 370 was a temporary provision and the President could issue the 2019 order under Art. 370(3)
Directed restoration of statehood 'at the earliest' and elections to J&K Assembly by 30 September 2024
explanation: Presidential Orders C.O. 272 (2019) and C.O. 273 (2019) abrogated special status. The Court also upheld the Union's power to reorganise J&K into a Union Territory (Ladakh as a separate UT).

title: Separation of Powers
points: Montesquieu's doctrine; India follows a functional (not strict) separation
Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955): India does not recognise strict separation
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): separation of powers is part of the basic structure
Article 50 (DPSP): separate judiciary from the executive in public services
explanation: Legislature makes law, executive implements it, judiciary interprets and adjudicates. In India overlap exists (e.g., ministers sit in Parliament; courts can issue guidelines under Art. 142).

title: Public Interest Litigation (PIL)
points: Relaxation of locus standi; pioneered by Justice P.N. Bhagwati & V.R. Krishna Iyer
Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979): first reported PIL (undertrials)
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981): any public-spirited person may move the court
Epistolary jurisdiction: letters treated as writ petitions
explanation: PIL lets any member of the public approach the court for the enforcement of public rights of persons who cannot do so themselves. Courts discourage 'publicity interest litigation' and have imposed costs for frivolous PILs.

title: Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)
points: Added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985; 91st Amendment (2003) removed the 'one-third split' exemption
Presiding officer (Speaker/Chairman) decides disqualification
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): upheld validity; Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review
explanation: A legislator is disqualified if they voluntarily give up party membership or vote/abstain contrary to the party whip. Exceptions: merger with another party (two-thirds of legislators).

title: Article 142 — Complete Justice
points: Allows the Supreme Court to pass any order necessary to do 'complete justice' in any case pending before it
Used in Union Carbide (1991), Ayodhya (2019) and many others
Cannot be used to override express statutory provisions or substantive law (Supreme Court Bar Association, 1998)
explanation: Article 142 is a unique power of the Supreme Court; critics call it 'judicial overreach' when used to fill legislative gaps.

title: Ordinances (Art. 123 & 213)
points: President (Art. 123) / Governor (Art. 213) may promulgate ordinances when the legislature is not in session
Must be laid before the legislature; ceases 6 weeks after reassembly
D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): 'ordinance raj' — re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution
Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): ordinances must be laid and re-promulgation is unconstitutional
explanation: An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament but is temporary, and is subject to the same limits (cannot violate Fundamental Rights).

title: Money Bill (Art. 110) & Finance Bill
points: Can be introduced only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation
Rajya Sabha may only recommend changes within 14 days; Speaker's certificate is final
Aadhaar Act (2016) was upheld as a Money Bill by a 4:1 majority in Puttaswamy II (2018) — dissent by Justice Chandrachud
explanation: Misuse of the 'money bill' route to bypass the Rajya Sabha has been challenged; the question was referred to a larger bench (Rojer Mathew, 2019).

title: Federalism & President's Rule
points: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): federalism is a basic feature; President's Rule is subject to judicial review
Floor test is the way to test majority — not the Governor's subjective view
Article 356 — failure of constitutional machinery in a State; Article 365 — failure to comply with Union directions
explanation: India is described as 'quasi-federal' (Art. 1: 'Union of States'). Bommai curbed misuse of Art. 356: proclamation can be judicially reviewed and Assemblies cannot be dissolved before Parliament approves.

title: Death Penalty — 'Rarest of Rare'
points: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980): 5-judge bench upheld constitutionality, death only in the 'rarest of rare' cases
Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983): mandatory death sentence (Sec. 303 IPC) struck down
Shatrughan Chauhan (2014): undue delay in deciding mercy petitions can be ground for commutation
explanation: Courts must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances and give 'special reasons' for awarding death.

title: Fundamental Rights — overview
points: Part III (Arts 12–35): Equality (14–18), Freedom (19–22), Exploitation (23–24), Religion (25–28), Cultural & Educational (29–30), Remedies (32)
Right to Property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) → Art. 300A
Article 12 'State' defined; Article 13 voids inconsistent laws
explanation: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, enforceable against the State (some, like Arts 15(2), 17, 23, 24, also against individuals) and subject to reasonable restrictions.

title: DPSP & Fundamental Duties
points: DPSP: Part IV (Arts 36–51) — non-justiciable; borrowed from the Irish Constitution
Fundamental Duties: Article 51A, Part IVA, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; 11 duties (11th added by 86th Amendment, 2002)
Minerva Mills (1980): harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is a basic feature
explanation: DPSPs guide the State in policy-making (e.g., Art. 39A free legal aid, Art. 44 Uniform Civil Code, Art. 48A environment).

title: Sedition & Free Speech
points: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962): sedition upheld but limited to incitement to violence
S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (May 2022): Supreme Court put Section 124A IPC in abeyance
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) drops the term 'sedition' and introduces Section 152 (acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India)
explanation: Article 19(2) lists reasonable restrictions on free speech: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of State, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence, etc.
